BIT 5534 Applied Business Intelligence and Analytics
Week 4 · Lecture 1
Principal component analysis, scores and loadings
Duration: 75 minutes · Platform: Hokie AI · Submission: Thread exported as a .txt and uploaded to Canvas before leaving class · Lecture Mode: exploratory
Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

  1. Say why columns that measure the same thing from nearby positions carry the same information twice, and where that repetition shows up in the correlation matrix.
  2. State what makes a direction special to a matrix, and find the eigenvalues of a two by two matrix from its characteristic polynomial.
  3. Say what standardizing does to a column and why the analysis then runs on the correlation matrix.
  4. Compute a score and a loading from an eigenvector, and say which of the two gives one number per row and which gives one number per column.
  5. Specify and build a tool that runs the analysis and draws its eigenvalues, its scores and its loadings, then check it against eigenvalues that are printed on the page.
Section 1 of 5
INTRODUCTION
📋 Note for Students

Three weeks of this course have fitted a model to a column you were trying to predict. Today nothing is being predicted. Twenty columns arrive with no target attached, they overlap heavily, and the work is finding out how much is actually in them.

The columns come off a plant floor. Twenty acoustic monitors are bolted around a bay a hundred meters on a side, and every time something happens on the floor each monitor reports how far away it thinks the event was. A thousand events are on file. The floor itself has two dimensions and the file has twenty columns, and the hour is about the gap between those two numbers.

Twenty acoustic monitors sit around a plant floor a hundred meters on a side. Every time something happens down there, each monitor reports how far away it thinks the event was, and it is wrong by about a quarter either way. A thousand events are on file.

An event counts as reachable when the response crew can get to it from the central station inside the target. Crews walk the aisles, so the distance that matters is measured along the grid, and the set of reachable points comes out as a diamond. It covers half the floor.

Two monitors standing near each other watch the same events from nearly the same place, so their columns say nearly the same thing. The correlation matrix is where the repetition shows up.

Every pair of the twenty is below, one hundred and ninety of them on one square. The average absolute correlation is 0.41, so the repetition runs across the whole set.

💬 Discussion

Two questions before any mathematics:

  • Two numbers would be enough to say where an event happened on the floor. You have twenty columns. What are the other eighteen doing?
  • You are allowed to build one new column out of all twenty, any way you like. What would you want it to measure?
Section 2 of 5
DEMONSTRATION

A matrix takes a vector and hands back another vector. Almost every vector comes back pointing somewhere else. A few come back pointing exactly where they started, longer or shorter but on the same ray, and those few are the ones this method is built on.

The determinant gives a polynomial in lambda whose degree is the size of the matrix, so a matrix with twenty rows has twenty roots and twenty directions. Nobody writes that polynomial down. A routine finds the roots, and the word eigen is German for of itself, which is what these are: properties the matrix carries whatever you do to it.

The matrix this method feeds on is the correlation matrix of your columns. It is square, it has ones down its diagonal, and every other entry is a correlation between two of your columns.

The left quantity is a score and the right quantity is a loading, and the panel names both. A thousand events give a thousand scores on the first component and a thousand more on the second, and plotting one against the other puts every event somewhere on a page. Twenty columns give twenty loadings on the first component and twenty on the second, and plotting those puts every monitor somewhere on a page. The score plot is about the events AND the loadings plot is about the monitors. Both.

💬 Discussion

Carry these into your own run:

  • Your file has two hundred and ten numbers in its correlation matrix and the floor has two dimensions. Three eigenvalues came back large. Where might a third direction have come from?
  • The score plot puts the reachable events in the middle and the rest around the edge, with a wide band where the two mix. Is that band the method losing information, or is it events near the edge of the diamond being genuinely hard to tell apart?

Class material
The bullets you send
I want a Python script that runs principal component analysis on a data file and shows everything in one window. I open it by double clicking it, and it should also take a file path as a command line argument so I can run it from a terminal.

Here is what it has to do.

- Read a .csv or an .xlsx file that I pick from a standard file open dialog.
- Offer me the numeric columns from that file and let me choose which of them go into the analysis. A column that is not numeric is never offered as an analysis variable.
- Let me nominate one column as an optional label. The label colors the points and the analysis never uses it. The tool works with no label chosen.
- Standardize every chosen column by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, so the analysis runs on the correlation matrix.
- Report every eigenvalue, its percent of the total, and its cumulative percent.
- Draw the eigenvalues as a bar chart, one bar per component, with the cumulative percent drawn over the bars as a line on its own axis. Beside the bars, tabulate the eigenvalue, the percent and the cumulative percent, with each row of the table sitting level with its own bar.
- Draw a score plot of the observations, where I choose which principal component goes on the horizontal axis and which goes on the vertical axis.
- Draw a loadings plot of the variables with every variable labeled, using the eigenvector components scaled by the square root of their eigenvalue.
- Never silently change a choice I have made. Once I pick a component for an axis it stays picked until I change it, and rerunning the analysis does not reset it.
- Keep the file choice, the column choices, the axis choices, the table and every plot inside one main window. Do not open a second window for anything.
- Use pandas, numpy, matplotlib and tkinter, and nothing else.

Ask me one question at a time about anything I have left unsettled, at most five questions, then write the finished prompt. Write no code until I send that finished prompt back to you.
Paste this into the M block once, unedited. It names the analysis and the four things the tool has to draw, and it ends by capping the interview at five questions. It is deliberately silent about how any of it looks on screen, and settling that is your job.

DISCUSSION

Class material
If your build did not finish
pca_explorer.py plant_floor.py
The first one does what the bullets asked for, and a tool you did not write still teaches the reading. The second is the simulator from the start of class, which draws a new floor whenever you ask it to and writes out its own file. If a download opens as text in your browser and does not save, right click the button and choose Save link as. If a script will not start, install what it needs with py -m pip install pandas numpy matplotlib openpyxl on Windows, or python3 -m pip install pandas numpy matplotlib openpyxl on a Mac.

Run it on plant_monitors. Every m column goes into the analysis AND reachable is the label AND reachable never enters the analysis itself.

Before you look at any picture, read the eigenvalues. You are looking for 7.2235, 6.4288 and 3.8797, and for all twenty to sum to 20. If your numbers differ, your tool made a decision you did not ask for, and the first place to look is whether it standardized the columns.

The score plot puts one point on the page for every event and the loadings plot puts one arrow for every monitor. Read both, and say what each one is placing.

Scroll back to the three pair pictures in section 1 and hold them next to your own score plot. Two columns at a time gave you a cigar and a cloud. Twenty at a time gave you this.

Then change something. Put PC3 on the vertical axis of the score plot and look at the colors again.

Check that the change actually took. A control that is on the screen and does nothing is a common way for a generated tool to fail, and it fails quietly, because the picture you are looking at is a perfectly good picture of the wrong two components. The axis labels on the plot are the honest report. Read those.

Both components are position. PC1 and PC2 between them say where on the floor an event happened, in a frame of their own choosing that is turned and flipped against east and north. Nothing told the tool where the monitors are or that there was a floor at all, and it recovered the layout from twenty columns of distances.

The loadings plot is the other half of that. It places each monitor by the direction that monitor sits in from the floor, so the twenty arrows come out as a map of the monitors, turned over the same way. On the demonstration file the two can be compared, since the monitor positions are known there. On your own file you have no map to check against, which is the ordinary situation.

Two is a fact about the plant. Three is a fact about twenty columns of distances. Neither one is wrong.

A monitor never reports where an event was. It reports how far away it was, and those are not the same kind of number. Walk east across the floor and your position changes at a steady rate the whole way. Your distance from a monitor standing out on the floor does something else: it falls while you are heading towards that monitor and rises once you are past it. Twenty monitors, twenty different places to be past, and the twenty columns end up carrying something the floor itself does not have.

The simulator is on this page and it will settle this for you. Open it, pull the noise down to zero, push the monitor spread out to 10 so every monitor is far away from the floor, press Write CSV, and run your own tool on the file it writes. Look at what the third eigenvalue does. Thursday starts there.

💬 Discussion

Take these into the reflection:

  • Your twenty arrows are scattered around the loadings plot and not piled on top of each other. What does that tell you that the correlation matrix did not?
  • The first two components turned out to mean position on the floor. Look at which events sit high on PC3 and which sit low, and say what you think that third one is measuring.
  • Nothing in your tool was told that there is a floor, or where any monitor sits. What did it use instead?
Section 5 of 5
REFLECTION

Now write your reflection, in your own words and without help from the AI.

Your reflection needs all four of these. Say how your score plot compares with the three pair pictures in section 1, and what you can see in one that you cannot see in the others AND say why your eigenvalues add to 20 and not to some other number AND say what the loadings plot shows and how that differs from what the score plot shows AND say whether you would report this floor as 2D or 3D, why, and what would change your mind.

The fourth is the one that separates a good reflection from an adequate one. Either number is a fine answer here. Three, because three eigenvalues stand well above the rest, is as good as two, because the floor is a floor. What is being marked is your reason, and whether you can say what evidence would move you off it.

Write 80 to 160 words.
